name: Transcutaneous lower blepharoplasty

lead: Transcutaneous lower blepharoplasty is a cosmetic operation on the lower eyelids. The surgeon makes a cut through the skin just under the lash line, then removes or moves the bulging orbital fat, tightens muscle where needed and trims extra skin. It is typically chosen when there is real skin laxity, not just fat pads.

The appearance payoff is a smoother lid-cheek transition with less puffiness and fewer creases, which can make the eyes look more rested. Surgical series report significant improvement in eye-bag severity, and modern techniques focus on preserving or repositioning volume and supporting the outer corner of the eye.

paras: The procedure is usually done as an outpatient operation under local or general anaesthesia, takes one to three hours, and may be combined with fat transposition, fat grafting, midface work or canthal support. The skin sutures are removed within several days, and swelling and bruising settle over several weeks.

Reported risks include lower eyelid malposition (lid pulled down or outward), visible or widened scars, dry eye, asymmetry and the need for revision. Surgeons use techniques such as lateral canthal support and muscle suspension to reduce malposition, and surgeons' series report low complication rates with these refinements.

chain: Fat repositioned or removed and skin trimmed
Smoother lid-cheek contour with fewer bags and creases
angle.text: The operation physically removes or relocates the fat and skin that cause lower-lid bags and creases. People use it to change under-eye contour, and surgeons often add support at the outer corner so the lid holds its position.

lead: Transcutaneous lower blepharoplasty, also called the external or subciliary approach, is a lower eyelid operation in which the incision is made in the skin just beneath the eyelashes. Through it the surgeon can remove or reposition orbital fat, excise skin and modify the orbicularis oculi muscle [1][2]. It is the standard counterpart to the transconjunctival approach, which works from inside the eyelid and leaves no external scar; Wikipedia notes that the skin-incision route is typically used when there is significant skin laxity [2].

People choose it to reduce under-eye bags, smooth crepey skin and soften the tear trough, so that the eyes look less tired. Looksmaxxing communities discuss it among eye-area surgeries, alongside transconjunctival fat repositioning, tear trough filler and canthoplasty.

The surgical literature is large. Recent reviews advocate fat preservation or transposition to avoid a hollowed look [1][3], and a 2026 review argues the transcutaneous approach suits almost all patients [4].

paras: The surgeon marks and incises the skin just below the lashes. Through it, orbital fat can be removed or moved into the tear trough, redundant skin trimmed, and the muscle adjusted. Techniques include fat transposition with preservation of volume [1][3], orbicularis suspension flaps [1][5], release of the orbicularis retaining ligament [6], and lateral canthal support to resist lid descent [7].
Terminology: the word blepharoplasty was coined by Karl Ferdinand von Gräfe in 1818, and Celsus described skin excision for eyelids in the first century [2].

The transconjunctival route leaves no visible scar and is used where there is little or no excess skin; where skin laxity exists, skin removal or other procedures are added [2]. One 2021 review presents transcutaneous surgery with volume preservation alongside transconjunctival repositioning and fat grafting as alternatives, with indications and contraindications for each [3]. A 2019 report described treating excess lower-lid skin without incisions as a separate option [8].

A 10-year review of primary transcutaneous lower blepharoplasty with routine lateral canthal support addressed the known association of this approach with lower lid malposition [7]. A study of 408 patients reported significant improvement of eye-bag severity across all age groups with a modified subciliary technique, with outcomes related to dynamic wrinkle number and dermal fibre density [9]. A 2026 article describing the 'X3' technique combines fat transposition, ligament release and three-vector suspension and reports durable improvement and low complication rates in a large series [4].

A randomised double-blind trial of 40 adults found botulinum toxin injected at the time of surgery was assessed for its effect on subciliary scar quality [10]. A randomised trial compared Colorado microdissection needle with scalpel incision for eyelid surgery [11]. Research on tear dynamics after the procedure has used optical coherence tomography [12].

The best-documented risk is lower lid malposition, which surgeons try to prevent with canthal support [7]. A literature on correcting palpebral fissure shape after previous lower blepharoplasty exists for people whose lids were altered [13]. Scarring can be wider in some patients, and trials have tested toxin for scar quality [10]. Other reported issues include contour irregularity, such as infraorbital grooves treated by fat injection [14]. Surgeons stress patient selection and technique.

timeline.event: Karl Ferdinand von Gräfe coins the term blepharoplasty [2].
Transcutaneous lower blepharoplasty is described in Facial Plastic Surgery [15].
